title: Design a Food Delivery System
summary: A three-sided marketplace of customer, restaurant, and courier, held together by one order record and a real-time state machine — batching orders onto one courier trip is the twist ride-hailing doesn't have.

slides.markdown:
The ask: a customer orders from a restaurant, a courier picks it up and delivers it, and all three parties — customer, restaurant, courier — see accurate, live status the whole way through.

Unlike [ride-hailing](design-ride-hailing-system), which matches two sides point-to-point, this is a **three-sided marketplace**: the restaurant has to accept and prepare the order before a courier assignment even makes sense, and a courier is often juggling more than one order at once.

The interesting design decisions live in that three-way handoff and in batching — not in a point-to-point match.

**Functional:** browse a restaurant's menu, place an order, get a prep-time estimate, get assigned a courier, track live status until delivery.

**Non-functional:** courier assignment latency low enough that food doesn't sit cold waiting for pickup; order accuracy (right items, right restaurant, right address) since errors here can't be silently retried like a failed API call; prep-time estimates accurate enough that a courier doesn't arrive 15 minutes before or after the food is ready.

The tension to name: batching orders onto one courier trip improves courier efficiency and pay-per-trip economics, but it can add delay to any single order in the batch — that trade-off is the crux of this design.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: orders, couriers, and batching windows
slides.markdown:
A mid-size city might have 5,000 concurrent orders in flight during a lunch peak, served by maybe 2,000 couriers online in that area — roughly 2.5 orders per courier if perfectly load-balanced, though real distribution is lumpy (some zones are far busier than others).

A batching window of even 60-90 seconds, applied to orders from restaurants close to each other, can turn what would be 2 separate courier trips into 1 — at city scale during peak hours, that's a meaningful multiplier on effective courier capacity without adding a single courier. The batching window is the key lever, and it's a scheduling problem, not a raw-throughput one.

Three calls anchor the three-sided flow:

- `placeOrder(customerId, restaurantId, items)` — creates the order and starts the state machine.
- `updateOrderStatus(orderId, status)` — called by the restaurant (accepted, preparing, ready) and the courier (picked up, delivered); every party reads from the same order record rather than each side maintaining its own copy.
- `assignCourier(orderId)` — internal call the assignment engine makes once an order is ready or near-ready, optionally batching it with a nearby order.

The shared design point: there's exactly one order record all three parties read and write against — no independent per-party copies to keep in sync.

slides.sectionTitle: Data model: the order state machine
slides.markdown:
An order moves through a strict sequence: `placed → accepted → preparing → ready for pickup → picked up → delivered` (with `cancelled` reachable from most early states). Modeling this as an explicit state machine — not a free-text status column — means every transition can be validated: a restaurant can't mark an order `delivered`, and a courier can't `pick up` an order that isn't `ready`.

This matters because three different actors are writing to the same record; without enforced transitions, a race (courier marks picked-up while the restaurant is simultaneously marking cancelled) can leave the order in a nonsensical or ambiguous state that support teams then have to untangle by hand.

![One shared order record with two-way arrows to customer, restaurant, and courier apps — a star, not a triangle](assets/order-star-topology.svg)

Customer, restaurant, and courier apps never talk to each other directly — each only reads and writes the shared order record, and each is pushed updates whenever it changes.

This star topology (not a triangle of direct connections) is what keeps the three views consistent: there's one source of truth, not three copies that could drift apart.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: per-order assignment vs batched courier routes
slides.markdown:
| | Assign per order | Batch multiple orders per courier |
|---|---|---|
| Courier efficiency | One trip per order — lower orders-per-hour per courier | One trip covers 2-3 orders from nearby restaurants — higher courier throughput |
| Delivery speed for one order | Fastest possible for that single order | Can add a few minutes if it's not first in the batch's route |
| Complexity | Simple: assign nearest available courier | Needs a routing decision — which orders batch well together (nearby restaurants, compatible ready-times) |
| Best fit | Low order density, or premium/fast-delivery tiers | Dense urban areas with many concurrent orders from clustered restaurants |

**How to decide:** batch when order density in an area is high enough that nearby restaurants' ready-times overlap — batching a courier across two orders that are nowhere near each other just adds delay for no efficiency gain.

![One courier route batching two nearby orders in a single trip, versus two separate unbatched courier trips](assets/order-batching.svg)

Batching only pays off when the ready-times and locations of two orders overlap enough that one courier's route barely lengthens by taking both.

A batching engine that ignores this and forces together orders from restaurants ten minutes apart just delays both without any of the efficiency benefit.

assets.alt: One courier route batching two nearby orders in a single trip, versus two separate unbatched courier trips

slides.sectionTitle: ETA prediction feeding both the customer and the assignment engine
slides.markdown:
ETA prediction serves two consumers with different needs. The **customer app** shows a single friendly countdown — it can afford some slack, since a slightly conservative estimate is better than one that's frequently wrong.

The **assignment engine** uses a sharper version of the same prediction to decide, in real time, whether an order is close enough to ready to start looking for a courier now, and whether a second order's ready-time is close enough to the first to justify batching them. An assignment decision made on a stale or overly-rounded ETA either sends a courier too early (they wait at the restaurant) or too late (food sits cold).

The takeaway: the same underlying prediction model can feed two different precision requirements — don't build two separate systems for it.

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: restaurant-side acceptance lag at lunch
slides.markdown:
During a lunch-hour spike, a single busy restaurant can receive far more simultaneous orders than its kitchen or staff can immediately acknowledge — even though the platform's own infrastructure has no trouble accepting the orders. The order sits in `placed` while a human at the restaurant is buried, and every downstream step (prep-time estimate, courier assignment) is blocked behind that acceptance.

This is a bottleneck the system can't purely engineer away — the fix is product-level: surfacing restaurant-side order-volume limits (so a slammed restaurant can temporarily throttle new orders) and giving restaurants a fast, low-friction accept action, rather than trying to force faster acceptance through backend tuning alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: syncing status via client polling
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Each app can just poll the order status every few seconds — simple and good enough."

**Why it's wrong:** polling means every client is showing a status that's stale by up to the polling interval, and at scale, three apps (customer, restaurant, courier) polling for every in-flight order multiplies into enormous read load for information that's mostly unchanged between polls — most of that load is wasted work.

**Correct model:** push status changes to subscribed clients the moment they happen — a WebSocket connection or push-notification channel per active order — so status is accurate in near real time and read load scales with actual state changes, not with a fixed polling interval times every client.
